title: Study
tomorrow: who do you call when the faith gets lonely?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: regular mercy, service written on the calendar instead of left to mood. That rule was for the hands. Today's piece is for the mind.

After five years on this path, is there anything left to learn? Ask a man in a garden in Milan. He's a grown man, a trained teacher of speech, and he has thrown himself down under a fig tree, crying, because he can't change the life he's living. Then, from a house nearby, a child's voice, singing the same words over and over, like a game. He gets up, walks back to where he left a book of Paul's letters, and opens it wherever it falls. What's on the page?
screen: `ANYTHING LEFT TO LEARN?` → `UNDER A FIG TREE, CRYING.` → `A CHILD'S VOICE. HE OPENS THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The man is Augustine, and he tells it himself in his Confessions. In Pusey's old translation, the child's song is "Take up and read; Take up and read." The book falls open at Paul's letter to the Romans, and the line he reads ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He writes that he didn't need to read any further. That's the famous part. Here's the part that's easy to miss: the garden wasn't the end of his reading. It was the start. Augustine kept reading, asking and writing for the rest of his life, and the Confessions itself is full of questions he's still working out, about memory, about time. For Catholics, study isn't a class you finish at Confirmation. Jesus names it in the great commandment: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind." The whole mind, too. One to tell a friend tonight: Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, wrote that not knowing the Scriptures is not knowing Christ. So a rule for life keeps a next book. Not a library. One book, picked on purpose, read a little at a time, the way Augustine started: one page.
screen: `TAKE UP AND READ.` · `PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.` · `HE KEPT READING FOR LIFE.` · `LOVE GOD WITH THY WHOLE MIND.` · then, large: `KEEP LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Grab a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the title of one book you'll read next: a gospel, a saint's life, the Catechism, a book someone you trust keeps pressing on you. Sit with the title in front of you, and if you pray, ask for the grace to keep turning pages.
Study. Loving God with the whole mind, one book at a time, the way a voice over a garden wall got a man reading.
Hold onto this: keep learning, because the garden was Augustine's first page, not his last. See you tomorrow.

Milan.meaning: a city in northern Italy, where Augustine was living

Augustine.meaning: a North African bishop and saint who wrote the Confessions

Confessions.meaning: Augustine's own story of his life and conversion, written as a prayer

Jerome.meaning: a saint and scholar who translated the Bible into Latin

Confirmation.meaning: the sacrament that seals baptism with the gift of the Holy Spirit
